Nothing issues from this step that could be altered, varied or appealed.
Nothing in the Environment Act reaches beyond the Manitoba segment, while NuPPAA ss.98 and 156–157 reach the whole project.
Above 230 kV is Class 3 and the Minister decides; 115 to 230 kV is Class 2 and the Director does. The voltage has not been published.

Environment Act s.14: the Director (or Minister) decides alone whether a change to a licensed development is minor; a minor alteration is approved in writing with no public comment, only a copy filed in the registry (s.14(2.1)), and anything larger goes back as a new proposal (s.14(3)).
Canadian Energy Regulator Act s.261: whether a federal decision-maker exists at all turns on this one order, and none has been made.
The order is not an assessment of anything, and no recorded concern can enter it.
NuPPAA s.156 applies the planning provisions to the entire project, including the segment outside Nunavut.
Conformity is tested against the text of the applicable land use plan and nothing else.
NuPPAA s.157 applies the screening provisions to the entire project.
The Board may determine that the project be modified or abandoned.
Section 90(i) makes cumulative impacts of any other project mandatory, and socio-economic impacts sit inside the statutory test itself.
Section 75(2) makes any permit issued before assessment is complete of no force or effect, not merely irregular.
Section 94(1)(a)(ii) makes a federal panel the default where the project is partly outside Nunavut; s.94(1)(a)(iii) lets the Board review it instead by agreement.
NuPPAA ss.93–94: the Minister selects the review body and may send a project to review even where the Board found none necessary.
NuPPAA ss.99 and 101: the guidelines tell the proponent what the assessment must cover.
The guidelines are deliberative, published in draft and open to comment — the same framing move as route selection, done in the open.
NuPPAA ss.160–162: the only body on this map with a mandate over the full 1,200 km corridor, including the Manitoba segment.
NuPPAA s.103 factors include (c) the priorities and values of the residents and (f) cumulative effects; s.103(3) admits traditional knowledge.
The test turns on the strength of the claim and the seriousness of the impact, so concerns not attaching to a right fall outside it however strongly held.
No statutory requirement to give reasons was found, and the provincial consultation policy has not been retrieved.
Each department reviews within its own mandate, and no step weighs the departmental views against one another.
No content filter appears in the Act, so anything may be said — and nothing determines what follows from it.
Section 12.0.1 requires proponent consultation to be considered and s.12.0.2 requires climate; how either is weighed against anything else is not specified.
An Environment Act appeal goes to the minister responsible for the issuing department; the provision has not been retrieved.

Environment Act s.27: anyone affected may appeal a Director’s licence decision to the Minister within 30 days; the Minister may dismiss, vary or quash it, or send it back (s.27(2)). A Minister’s own decision is appealed to cabinet (s.28). No independent tribunal.
Habitat is assessed against standards with offsetting, and nothing else is admitted.
The Nunavut Agreement articles and the regional association's lands policy have not been retrieved.
Whether the permit or lease can be revisited, and whether any of it is public, is unclear.

One project runs through two processes with no step joining them. Coordinating machinery exists on both sides — NuPPAA ss.159 and 162, the Environment Act s.13.1, the Joint Environmental Assessment Regulation 126/91 — and none of it has been used here.
